implementation_notes: In browsers and workers navigator.locks is a genuine implicit lock: request() acquires the named lock for the origin, runs the callback with it and releases it when the returned promise settles, which MDN states as 'the lock is automatically released when the task completes' - so there is no unlock call to forget and the critical section may await. Modes (exclusive/shared), ifAvailable and steal provide the policy knobs, and holder/title metadata make the lock observable. It coordinates tabs and workers (leader election, storage sync) rather than protecting shared memory, and Node services get the same effect from database transactions or an async-mutex library.
pitfalls: The callback may be async, so a hung promise holds the lock indefinitely and other tabs wait forever; combine a timeout or AbortSignal with the callback.
Lock granularity is a string name in one origin: a typo locks nothing, and two unrelated subsystems sharing a name serialize each other for as long as their critical sections last.
navigator.locks exists in browsers and workers, not in Node; and it protects coordination, not SharedArrayBuffer memory, which needs Atomics.

variants.name: using declarations with Symbol.dispose guards
variants.idiom_name: using guard = acquire(m); / await using guard = await acquire(m);
variants.implementation_notes: The structural half on the language side: a using declaration disposes its value when the variable goes out of scope, so a guard object whose [Symbol.dispose]() releases the mutex makes release a property of the block, the same shape C# gets from using. Mutex libraries expose it directly (a scope-returning acquire, or an async-mutex style runExclusive wrapped in a guard), and TypeScript 5.2 downlevels using for older targets. It yields block-scoped critical sections in a single-threaded runtime, where the hazard is interleaving rather than data races.
pitfalls: using must be initialized in place and the value must implement Symbol.dispose; a plain object without it throws, and reassignment is a syntax error.
Holding a mutex across an await serializes unrelated async work, and library mutexes are not reentrant: calling back into code that takes the same lock deadlocks.
Single-threaded JavaScript has no data races, so a mutex prevents interleaving only; shared memory across workers must use Atomics, which cannot be made implicit.
